questions.title: ISNULL vs. COALESCE vs. NULLIF
questions.prompt: In T-SQL, what's the difference between ISNULL(), COALESCE(), and NULLIF(), and when would you actually reach for each one on the job?
questions.code:
SELECT ISNULL(DiscountPct, 0), COALESCE(DiscountPct, StandardDiscount, 0), NULLIF(DiscountPct, 0)
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;
questions.modelAnswer: ISNULL(expr, replacement) is a SQL Server-only function that takes exactly two arguments and returns the first one if it isn't NULL, otherwise the second. Its return type is determined by the first argument, which can silently truncate a wider replacement value. COALESCE(expr1, ..., exprN) is the ANSI-standard equivalent, accepts any number of arguments, and returns the first non-NULL one, with its data type determined by precedence across all arguments supplied — that makes it more predictable and portable across SQL Server, Snowflake, Postgres, and other platforms this role touches. NULLIF(expr1, expr2) does the opposite job: it compares two expressions and returns NULL if they're equal, otherwise the first expression — the standard use is turning a known placeholder value like 0 into a real NULL so a division or aggregate doesn't quietly produce a wrong answer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I default to COALESCE for replacing NULLs because it works the same way across every platform I touch in this stack, not just SQL Server, and it lets me chain more than one fallback value in a row, which ISNULL can't do with just two arguments. I'll still use ISNULL inside a SQL-Server-only stored procedure where the slight performance edge or the shorter syntax doesn't matter much, but I don't reach for it out of habit. NULLIF comes up for a different reason entirely — usually when I'm dividing two columns and a denominator of 0 would blow up the query with a divide-by-zero error, so I wrap the denominator in NULLIF(Denominator, 0) to turn that zero into a NULL, which division handles gracefully by returning NULL instead of erroring.
commonMistakes: Assuming ISNULL and COALESCE are fully interchangeable instead of noticing COALESCE accepts more arguments and is cross-platform
Not realizing ISNULL's return type comes from its first argument, which can truncate a longer replacement string
Forgetting NULLIF compares for equality and returns NULL on a match, not the other way around
Writing a nested CASE expression to replace a NULL with a default instead of the much shorter COALESCE or ISNULL
keyPoints: ISNULL takes exactly two arguments and is SQL-Server-specific
COALESCE takes any number of arguments and is ANSI-standard/cross-platform
ISNULL's output type comes from its first argument and can truncate
NULLIF returns NULL when two expressions are equal, often used to prevent divide-by-zero

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes ISNULL from COALESCE
Correctly explains NULLIF's behavior and a real use case
Notes the portability/type-truncation nuance

questions.title: The CASE expression
questions.prompt: What is a CASE expression in T-SQL, and how does the searched form (CASE WHEN condition THEN ...) differ from the simple form (CASE column WHEN value THEN ...)?
questions.code:
SELECT Name,
  CASE WHEN ListPrice = 0 THEN 'Not for Sale'
       WHEN ListPrice < 50 THEN 'Budget'
       ELSE 'Premium' END AS PriceTier
FROM Production.Product;
questions.modelAnswer: A CASE expression returns a single value chosen from a set of conditional branches, and it can appear anywhere a regular expression can — in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, or even inside an aggregate. The simple form, CASE column WHEN value1 THEN result1 ... END, only tests one column for equality against a list of literal values, which is compact but limited. The searched form, CASE WHEN condition1 THEN result1 WHEN condition2 THEN result2 ... ELSE default END, allows any Boolean condition in each branch — ranges, comparisons across multiple columns, even subqueries — which is why it's used far more often in real reporting logic like bucketing a price into tiers. Conditions are evaluated top to bottom and the first one that's true wins, so order matters, and an ELSE branch should generally be included to avoid an unexpected NULL when nothing matches.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of the simple CASE as a shortcut for 'if this one column equals this value' and the searched CASE as the general-purpose version that can test any condition, including ranges and multiple columns at once, which is why I use the searched form constantly and the simple form only occasionally. The thing I always watch for is evaluation order — CASE checks branches top to bottom and stops at the first true one, so if I accidentally put a broader condition before a narrower one, the narrower one never gets a chance to fire. I also make it a habit to always add an ELSE, even if it's just ELSE 'Other', because without one, any row that doesn't match a WHEN silently comes back as NULL, and that's an easy thing to miss in a report until someone asks why a bucket is empty.
commonMistakes: Putting a broader WHEN condition before a narrower one, so the narrower branch can never fire
Leaving off the ELSE branch and being surprised when non-matching rows return NULL
Trying to test a range or multiple columns using the simple CASE form instead of the searched form
Confusing CASE (an expression returning a value) with an IF statement (a control-flow block)
keyPoints: CASE is an expression that returns one value, usable anywhere an expression can appear
Simple CASE tests one column for equality; searched CASE allows any Boolean condition
Branches evaluate top to bottom; the first true one wins
Always include ELSE to avoid unexpected NULLs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes simple vs. searched CASE
Explains top-to-bottom evaluation order
Mentions the importance of ELSE

questions.title: Fact tables vs. dimension tables
questions.prompt: In a star schema, what's the difference between a fact table and a dimension table, and what kinds of columns would you expect to find in each?
questions.modelAnswer: A fact table holds the measurable events of the business — things like sales transactions, order lines, or page views — and its rows are typically numeric and additive: quantity, amount, cost. Each fact row also carries a set of foreign keys pointing out to the dimension tables that give that event context. A dimension table holds the descriptive attributes used to filter, group, and label those facts — things like Customer, Product, Date, or Store — and its columns are mostly text or categorical attributes rather than numbers meant to be summed. The practical test is: if a column is something you'd aggregate (SUM, AVG, COUNT), it belongs in the fact table; if it's something you'd filter, slice, or group by, it belongs in a dimension. A well-designed star schema has one central fact table surrounded by several dimension tables joined to it by single-column surrogate keys, which keeps queries simple and fast.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the fact table as the 'what happened' table — every row is one event, like one line item on one order, and most of its columns are numbers I'll eventually sum or average. The dimension tables are the 'who, what, when, where' tables that give that event meaning: the Customer dimension tells me who bought it, the Date dimension tells me when, the Product dimension tells me what. My rule of thumb when I'm not sure where a column belongs is to ask whether I'd ever aggregate it — if yes, it's a fact column; if I'd only ever filter or group by it, it's a dimension attribute. I also expect the fact table to be joined to each dimension through a simple surrogate key rather than a long natural key, since that keeps the joins fast and the model easy to extend later.
questions.example:
-- FactSales: SalesAmount, Quantity, DiscountAmount, plus FKs to DimDate/DimProduct/DimCustomer
-- DimProduct: ProductKey, ProductName, Category, Color, Size (descriptive, not summed)
commonMistakes: Putting a descriptive attribute like a product name directly in the fact table instead of a dimension
Treating a dimension's numeric-looking attribute (like a ZIP code) as something to sum rather than just a label
Forgetting that fact tables are usually much taller (more rows) while dimension tables are usually much wider (more columns)
Joining facts to dimensions on a long natural key instead of a short surrogate key
keyPoints: Fact table = measurable business events, mostly additive numeric columns
Dimension table = descriptive context used to filter/group/label
Rule of thumb: aggregate it -> fact; filter/group by it -> dimension
Facts join to dimensions via surrogate keys in a star schema

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes fact from dimension tables
Gives a usable rule of thumb for classifying a column
Mentions surrogate key joins

questions.title: SCD Type 1 vs. Type 2
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a Type 1 and a Type 2 slowly changing dimension, and why would a data warehouse ever need to track history instead of just overwriting a changed value?
questions.modelAnswer: A Type 1 slowly changing dimension simply overwrites the old attribute value with the new one — if a customer moves from Texas to Colorado, the row is updated in place and no record of Texas ever remains. That's fine when history genuinely doesn't matter and you only care about the current state. A Type 2 slowly changing dimension instead preserves history by inserting a brand-new row for the changed record rather than updating the old one — the old row is typically marked with an end date and an IsCurrent flag set to false, and the new row gets a new surrogate key, a start date, and IsCurrent set to true. This matters because a fact table row for a sale made while the customer still lived in Texas should still show Texas when you report on it later, even though the customer has since moved — overwriting with Type 1 would make it look like every past sale happened in Colorado, which misrepresents history.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain Type 1 as the 'just fix it' approach — the old value is gone the moment it changes, which is perfectly fine for something like correcting a typo in a customer's name. Type 2 is for when the history itself is the point: if a sales rep gets promoted from one territory to another halfway through the year, I don't want every historical sale from before the promotion to suddenly look like it happened under their new territory. So instead of updating that row, I insert a new row with a new surrogate key, flip the old row's IsCurrent flag off and give it an end date, and the new row becomes the current one. Any fact row recorded before the change keeps pointing at the old surrogate key, so historical reporting stays accurate, while new sales automatically pick up the new row through the active key.
questions.example:
-- Type 2: customer moves from TX to CO
-- Old row: CustomerKey=101, State='TX', IsCurrent=0, EndDate='2026-06-01'
-- New row: CustomerKey=205, State='CO', IsCurrent=1, EndDate=NULL
-- Past fact rows still point at CustomerKey=101, preserving history.
commonMistakes: Using Type 1 for an attribute where historical accuracy actually matters, silently rewriting history
Forgetting Type 2 requires a new surrogate key for the new row, not just a new value in the same row
Not maintaining the IsCurrent flag / end date, making it hard to find 'the current version' of a dimension row
Assuming every attribute in a dimension needs the same SCD treatment, instead of applying Type 1 or Type 2 per column based on business need
keyPoints: Type 1 overwrites the old value; no history is kept
Type 2 inserts a new row to preserve history, with a new surrogate key
Type 2 typically uses IsCurrent flags and start/end dates to mark the active row
Fact rows recorded before a change keep pointing at the old dimension row under Type 2

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes Type 1 from Type 2
Explains why history preservation matters with a concrete scenario
Mentions surrogate key / IsCurrent flag mechanics

questions.title: The EXISTS vs. IN NULL trap
questions.prompt: What's the difference between filtering with EXISTS and filtering with NOT IN against a subquery, and why can NOT IN silently return zero rows when the subquery's column contains a NULL?
questions.code:
SELECT Name FROM Production.Product
WHERE ProductID NOT IN (SELECT ProductID FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail);
questions.modelAnswer: EXISTS checks whether a subquery returns any rows at all for the current outer row, and it stops as soon as it finds one match — it never actually compares values against NULL, it just asks a yes/no question. IN and NOT IN, on the other hand, build a literal list of values from the subquery and compare the outer value against that list using equality logic. The trap is specifically with NOT IN: SQL uses three-valued logic, so comparing a value against a NULL in that list doesn't evaluate to false, it evaluates to unknown — and if even one NULL appears anywhere in the subquery's result, the entire NOT IN expression can evaluate to unknown for every row, which the WHERE clause treats the same as false, silently returning zero rows even when matches clearly should exist. NOT EXISTS doesn't have this problem because it never compares values directly; it only checks for row existence inside a correlated subquery. The safe practice is to either filter NULLs out of the subquery explicitly or default to NOT EXISTS/EXISTS instead of IN/NOT IN whenever NULLs might be present.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of those bugs that doesn't throw an error, it just quietly returns the wrong answer, which is exactly why I bring it up. If I write WHERE ProductID NOT IN (SELECT ProductID FROM SalesOrderDetail) and that subquery's ProductID column happens to contain even a single NULL, the whole NOT IN condition can collapse to unknown for every row, and I get an empty result set with no error message telling me why. EXISTS and NOT EXISTS avoid this entirely because they're not comparing values — they're just asking 'does at least one matching row exist,' which is a yes/no question that NULL can't poison. So as a habit, I reach for NOT EXISTS over NOT IN whenever there's any chance the subquery's column allows NULLs, which in practice is most of the time unless I've explicitly verified otherwise.
commonMistakes: Using NOT IN against a subquery without checking whether that column can contain NULL
Assuming a NULL in the subquery would just be skipped, rather than potentially poisoning the entire comparison
Not recognizing that an empty result from NOT IN with no error is itself a red flag worth investigating
Treating EXISTS and IN as always interchangeable instead of understanding the underlying three-valued-logic difference
keyPoints: EXISTS checks row existence; IN/NOT IN compares values against a literal list
SQL uses three-valued logic: true, false, and unknown
A NULL anywhere in a NOT IN subquery's result can make the whole condition unknown for every row
NOT EXISTS is immune to this because it never compares values directly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the NOT IN / NULL trap mechanism
Correctly contrasts EXISTS's existence-check behavior
Recommends a safe practice to avoid the trap

questions.title: Normalization basics: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF
questions.prompt: At a beginner level, what problem does normalization solve, and what does each of 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF add on top of the last?
questions.modelAnswer: Normalization organizes a database's tables to eliminate redundant data and the update/insert/delete anomalies that redundancy causes — if the same fact is stored in five places, updating it means finding and fixing all five, and missing even one leaves the database internally inconsistent. First normal form (1NF) requires every column to hold a single, atomic value — no comma-separated lists or repeating groups crammed into one cell — and every row must be uniquely identifiable. Second normal form (2NF) builds on 1NF by requiring every non-key column to depend on the entire primary key, not just part of it, which only becomes relevant with composite keys — a column that depends on just one part of a two-column key is a 2NF violation and should move to its own table. Third normal form (3NF) goes further and requires every non-key column to depend only on the primary key and nothing else — not on another non-key column — eliminating what's called a transitive dependency, like storing both a ZIP code and a city/state in an orders table when the city and state are fully determined by the ZIP code and arguably belong in their own lookup table.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core problem normalization solves is: if the same piece of information lives in multiple rows, I now have multiple places that can disagree with each other, and the database has no way of knowing which one is right. 1NF is the simplest rule — one value per cell, no lists jammed into a single column. 2NF only comes up once there's a composite primary key, and it just means every other column has to depend on the whole key, not half of it. 3NF is the one I think about most in practice: it says a non-key column can't depend on another non-key column — so if I've got a City and a ZIP code both sitting in the same table and City is fully determined by ZIP, that's a sign City might not belong there and should live in its own lookup table instead, with the orders table just referencing the ZIP.
commonMistakes: Storing a comma-separated list of values in one column, violating 1NF immediately
Not recognizing 2NF only applies when a composite (multi-column) primary key is involved
Confusing 3NF's transitive dependency rule with 2NF's partial dependency rule
Assuming more normalization is always better, without weighing the extra joins it requires at query time
keyPoints: Normalization reduces redundancy and the anomalies it causes
1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
2NF: every non-key column depends on the whole (composite) key
3NF: no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependency)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the redundancy problem normalization solves
Correctly describes 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF individually
Gives a concrete example of a violation

questions.title: Query folding in Power Query
questions.prompt: What is query folding in Power Query, and why does the order in which you apply transformation steps affect whether folding happens?
questions.modelAnswer: Query folding is Power Query's ability to translate the transformation steps you build in the Power Query editor — filtering, removing columns, grouping, renaming — back into a single native query (SQL, for a relational source) that runs on the source system itself, rather than pulling all the raw data into Power BI first and then transforming it locally. When folding happens, the source database does the filtering and aggregating, which is dramatically faster and lighter on both the network and Power BI's own engine, especially against a large table. Folding can break partway through a query if you add a step that the source can't translate — a step using a Power-Query-only function, a call to another query, or certain custom-column logic — and once folding breaks at a given step, every step after it runs locally in Power BI's own engine instead, even if those later steps individually could have folded on their own. Because of that, a practical habit is to do the steps that fold well (filtering rows, removing columns, simple renames) as early as possible, before steps that are more likely to break folding.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of query folding as Power Query being smart enough to hand its work back to the source database instead of doing everything itself after dragging all the rows across the network first. When it's working, a filter I apply in the Power Query editor literally becomes a WHERE clause in the SQL query sent to the source, which is a huge difference in performance on a large table. The step order matters because folding is sequential — the moment one step can't be translated back to the source, every step after it falls back to running locally in Power BI, even if a later step on its own would have folded fine. So in practice I try to filter rows and drop unused columns as early as possible in my step list, and I save anything exotic — a custom M function, a merge with another non-foldable query — for as late as possible, to keep as much of the pipeline folding as I can.
commonMistakes: Assuming every Power Query step always folds back to the source regardless of order or complexity
Adding a custom-column or non-foldable step early, which breaks folding for every step after it
Not checking (via View Native Query) whether a query is actually folding before assuming performance is fine
Removing columns or filtering rows too late in the step order, after non-foldable steps have already broken folding
keyPoints: Query folding translates Power Query steps into a native query run on the source
Folding pushes filtering/aggregation work to the source instead of Power BI's local engine
Folding can break at a step the source can't translate; everything after that step runs locally
Ordering foldable steps (filter, remove columns) early preserves folding for longer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines query folding and its performance benefit
Explains why folding can break and what happens when it does
Gives a practical step-ordering recommendation

questions.title: Relationship cardinality in Power BI
questions.prompt: In Power BI's data model, what does a one-to-many relationship mean, and why does it matter which side is the 'one' and which is the 'many' when you're deciding how to build a model?
questions.modelAnswer: A one-to-many relationship means a single row on the 'one' side can relate to multiple rows on the 'many' side, but each row on the 'many' side relates to exactly one row on the 'one' side. In a typical star schema, the dimension table (like Product) is the 'one' side and the fact table (like Sales) is the 'many' side, because one product can appear on many sales rows, but each sales row belongs to exactly one product. Power BI enforces this by requiring the 'one' side's related column to contain unique values — it's effectively acting like a key for the relationship — while the 'many' side's column can repeat freely. This direction matters because filters naturally flow from the 'one' side to the 'many' side by default: filtering Product to a single color filters down to only the matching sales rows, which is the behavior almost every report depends on. If a model is accidentally built the other way, or as a many-to-many relationship, filtering stops behaving predictably and can silently produce inflated or incorrect totals.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the Product-to-Sales example, since it's the one every model eventually has. Product is the 'one' side because each product has one row in the Product table, but that same product can show up on dozens of rows in the Sales table, which is the 'many' side. Power BI actually requires the 'one' side to have unique values in that column, which is part of how it figures out the direction automatically when I build the relationship. The reason I care which side is which isn't academic — filters flow from one to many by default, so when a user clicks a product in a slicer, that filter flows down into Sales and only shows matching rows. If I ever end up with a many-to-many relationship instead, that clean one-directional filtering breaks down, and I usually treat that as a signal to rework the model with a proper bridge table rather than just accepting the default many-to-many behavior.
commonMistakes: Not realizing the 'one' side's column must contain unique values for the relationship to work as intended
Assuming filter direction is symmetric instead of flowing from one to many by default
Building a many-to-many relationship by accident instead of recognizing it needs a bridge table
Confusing which table is the dimension (one side) and which is the fact (many side) in a star schema
keyPoints: One-to-many: one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side
The 'one' side's related column must contain unique values
Dimension tables are typically the 'one' side; fact tables the 'many' side
Filters flow from the one side to the many side by default

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains one-to-many cardinality
Correctly identifies which side is which in a star schema
Explains the filter-direction consequence

questions.title: Tableau live connection vs. extract
questions.prompt: In Tableau, what's the difference between a live connection and an extract (the Hyper engine), and what factors would make you choose one over the other for a given dashboard?
questions.modelAnswer: A live connection sends a query directly to the source database every time a view is loaded or a filter changes, so the data is always as current as the source itself, but performance depends entirely on how fast that source can answer the query. An extract instead takes a snapshot of the data and stores it in Tableau's own highly compressed, columnar Hyper engine format, so dashboards built on it are typically much faster and don't hammer the source with repeated queries — the trade-off is that the data is only as fresh as the last extract refresh, and very large extracts take time and storage to build and refresh. The choice generally comes down to three questions: how fresh does the data need to be, how fast is the source at answering ad hoc queries, and how large is the dataset. A small, frequently updated source with a fast database often works fine live; a huge dataset or a slow source is usually a strong case for an extract with a scheduled refresh.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as freshness versus speed. A live connection means every click in the dashboard re-queries the actual source, so it's always current, but it's only as fast as that source — if the source is a slow, heavily used transactional database, a live-connected dashboard can feel sluggish and also adds query load onto a system that probably has other jobs to do. An extract takes a compressed snapshot into Tableau's own Hyper format, which makes the dashboard noticeably snappier and takes load off the source entirely, but now I'm managing a refresh schedule, and users are looking at data that's only as current as the last refresh. In practice, for a reporting dashboard that gets used constantly throughout the day against a large table, I lean toward an extract with a nightly or hourly refresh; for something that genuinely needs to reflect what just happened, like an operational monitoring view, I'd keep it live even if that costs some speed.
commonMistakes: Assuming live connections are always 'more accurate' without weighing the performance cost on the source
Not scheduling extract refreshes, leaving a dashboard quietly showing stale data
Choosing an extract for a dataset too large to refresh in a reasonable window without first checking incremental refresh options
Forgetting that a live connection adds repeated query load directly onto the source system
keyPoints: Live connection queries the source directly every time; always current, speed depends on the source
Extract snapshots data into Tableau's Hyper engine; fast but only as fresh as the last refresh
Choice depends on required freshness, source speed, and data volume
Extracts need a scheduled refresh to stay usefully current

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the live vs. extract mechanics
Gives a sensible decision framework

questions.title: Linked services vs. datasets in Azure Data Factory
questions.prompt: In Azure Data Factory, what's the difference between a linked service and a dataset, and why does ADF separate these two concepts instead of combining them into one object?
questions.modelAnswer: A linked service is the connection information to a system — the server/account, authentication method (connection string, managed identity, or a Key Vault reference), and other connectivity details needed to reach that source or destination. A dataset is a named reference to a specific piece of data within that connection — a particular table, file, or folder path — along with its schema and format. ADF separates them because the relationship is naturally one-to-many: a single linked service to a SQL Server or storage account can back many different datasets (different tables, different files in different folders), so defining connection details once in the linked service and reusing it across many datasets avoids repeating the same credentials and connection logic over and over. It also makes maintenance far simpler — if a password or connection string changes, there's exactly one linked service to update, and every dataset built on top of it automatically picks up the change.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the linked service as 'how do I connect' and the dataset as 'what specific thing am I pointing at once I'm connected.' One linked service to an Azure SQL Database, for example, can back a dozen different datasets, each pointing at a different table, because the connection details don't change — only the specific object does. Keeping these separate is what makes maintenance manageable: if a connection string or a managed identity setup ever changes, I update it in exactly one place, the linked service, and every pipeline using any dataset built on top of it just keeps working without me having to hunt down a dozen hardcoded connection strings scattered across datasets.
commonMistakes: Assuming a linked service and a dataset are the same object instead of a one-to-many relationship
Hardcoding connection details inside a dataset instead of referencing a linked service
Not using Key Vault or managed identity for linked service credentials, falling back to plaintext connection strings
Creating a new linked service for every dataset instead of reusing one across many datasets pointing at the same system
keyPoints: Linked service = connection info to a system (how to connect)
Dataset = a specific table/file/path within that connection (what to point at)
One linked service can back many datasets
Separating them centralizes credential/connection maintenance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes linked service from dataset
Explains the one-to-many relationship and why it's useful
Mentions secure credential handling (Key Vault/managed identity)

questions.title: Snowflake's storage/compute separation
questions.prompt: What does it mean that Snowflake separates storage from compute, and why does that matter for a team where multiple people or workloads need to query the same data at once?
questions.modelAnswer: In Snowflake, data is stored once in a central, cloud-based storage layer, completely independent of the compute resources (virtual warehouses) that actually run queries against it. A virtual warehouse is a cluster of compute resources that can be resized, suspended, resumed, or spun up as an entirely separate warehouse, without touching the underlying stored data at all. Because storage and compute are decoupled, multiple virtual warehouses can query the exact same underlying data simultaneously without contending with each other for compute resources — a finance team's reporting warehouse and a data engineering team's ETL warehouse can both hit the same tables at the same time without slowing each other down, something that's much harder in a traditional database where storage and compute are tied to the same server. It also means compute can be scaled or shut off independently of storage: a warehouse can auto-suspend when idle to stop costing money, while the data it would have queried sits there unaffected, ready for the next warehouse that needs it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain this with the contention problem it solves. In a traditional database, if a heavy reporting query and a heavy ETL load both hit the same server at the same time, they compete for the same CPU and memory, and everyone's queries slow down together. Snowflake avoids that because storage is one shared layer and compute is a separate, resizable fleet of virtual warehouses — I could spin up one warehouse just for the BI team's dashboards and a completely separate one for an overnight load job, and because they're independent compute clusters, neither one starves the other, even though they're both reading and writing the same underlying tables. It also means I'm not paying for compute I'm not using — a warehouse can auto-suspend after a few minutes of inactivity, and the data itself doesn't disappear or become any less available just because the compute cluster that was reading it spun down.
commonMistakes: Assuming Snowflake works like a traditional database where storage and compute live on the same server
Not realizing multiple virtual warehouses can query the same data simultaneously without contention
Forgetting that resizing or suspending a warehouse has no effect on the underlying stored data
Thinking separating storage and compute means data is duplicated per warehouse, rather than shared
keyPoints: Storage is a single shared layer, independent of compute
Virtual warehouses are separate, resizable compute clusters
Multiple warehouses can query the same data concurrently without contention
Compute can scale or auto-suspend independently of storage, controlling cost

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the storage/compute separation

deepDive.heading: Why this architecture is worth understanding early
deepDive.content: A lot of candidates memorize 'Snowflake separates storage and compute' as a slogan without being able to explain why it's actually valuable. The concrete payoff is workload isolation: a company can run a dozen virtual warehouses of different sizes against the same tables at the same time, each sized for its own job, and none of them compete for the same hardware the way they would on a traditional single-server database. That's also why Snowflake billing is based on compute seconds, not storage access -- storage is billed separately and cheaply, while compute is billed per-second only while a warehouse is actively running, which is why AUTO_SUSPEND and AUTO_RESUME settings matter so much for cost control in a real environment.

questions.title: dbt's ref() function and the DAG
questions.prompt: What does dbt's ref() function actually do, and how does using it instead of hardcoding a table name let dbt build a dependency graph (DAG) of your models automatically?
questions.modelAnswer: ref() is how one dbt model refers to another model inside its SQL, instead of hardcoding a fully-qualified table name. At compile time, dbt resolves ref('stg_orders') into whatever the actual database, schema, and table name is for that model in the current environment — which means the same code works unchanged whether it's running in a dev schema, a staging schema, or production, since dbt figures out the right physical name each time. The bigger reason ref() matters is that it's how dbt builds its dependency graph: because every model declares its upstream dependencies through ref() calls rather than hardcoded names, dbt can parse the whole project and know exactly which models depend on which, which lets it run models in the correct order automatically and only rebuild what's actually downstream of something that changed. Hardcoding a table name instead of using ref() breaks this entirely — dbt has no way to see that dependency, so it can't guarantee the referenced model is built first, and documentation/lineage graphs lose that connection too.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain ref() as dbt's way of saying 'depend on this other model, not on a specific hardcoded table name.' When I write SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }} inside a downstream model, dbt swaps that in at compile time for whatever stg_orders actually resolves to in whichever environment I'm running in, so the same model code works in dev and in production without me touching it. The real payoff, though, is the DAG — because every ref() is a declared dependency, dbt can look at my whole project and figure out the correct build order on its own, run models in parallel where it's safe to, and when I only need to rebuild one model and everything downstream of it, dbt run --select stg_orders+ knows exactly what that means. If I'd hardcoded the table name instead of using ref(), none of that works -- dbt has no idea that dependency exists, so the build order isn't guaranteed and the lineage graph in the docs would be missing that connection entirely.
questions.example:
-- models/marts/fct_orders.sql
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }} o
JOIN {{ ref('stg_customers') }} c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id

Not realizing ref() is what lets dbt infer build order automatically rather than something declared separately
Confusing ref() (for other dbt models) with source() (for raw tables not built by dbt)
Assuming the DAG has to be manually configured somewhere instead of being inferred from ref()/source() calls
keyPoints: ref() resolves to the correct physical table name per environment at compile time
ref() calls are how dbt infers each model's upstream dependencies
dbt uses those dependencies to build a DAG and determine correct run order
Hardcoding table names instead of ref() breaks both portability and lineage

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what ref() resolves to and when
Correctly explains how ref() enables the DAG/run order
Notes the consequence of hardcoding instead of using ref()

questions.title: Pagination syntax across SQL dialects
questions.prompt: If you need to return just the top 10 rows of a result set, how does the syntax differ between T-SQL (TOP), Oracle (ROWNUM or FETCH FIRST), MySQL/Postgres (LIMIT), and the ANSI-standard OFFSET/FETCH clause, and why does this matter when moving between platforms in this stack?
questions.code:
-- T-SQL
SELECT TOP 10 Name, ListPrice FROM Production.Product ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
questions.modelAnswer: T-SQL uses SELECT TOP (n) at the very start of the column list, which is SQL-Server/Azure-SQL-specific syntax. MySQL and Postgres use LIMIT n (optionally with OFFSET n for pagination) at the end of the query, after ORDER BY. Oracle historically required filtering on the pseudo-column ROWNUM in a WHERE clause (a quirk because ROWNUM is assigned before ORDER BY sorts the rows, so getting the top N by some order required wrapping the query in a subquery first), though modern Oracle also supports the ANSI-standard FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY. That ANSI-standard OFFSET/FETCH syntax -- OFFSET n ROWS FETCH NEXT n ROWS ONLY -- is also supported in T-SQL as an alternative to TOP, and in Postgres, making it the most portable choice when a query needs to run unmodified across more than one of these platforms, which comes up constantly in this stack where the same logic might touch SQL Server, Snowflake, and a cloud warehouse. The practical risk is assuming any one syntax is universal -- a query hardcoded with TOP breaks the moment it's run against Postgres or Snowflake, and ROWNUM filtering breaks in a non-obvious way if you forget it's applied before sorting.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the syntax differences quickly since I've actually had to migrate queries between these platforms. TOP 10 is SQL Server's own syntax and sits right after SELECT. LIMIT 10 is what MySQL and Postgres use instead, tacked onto the end of the query. Oracle is the one that trips people up -- older Oracle code filters on ROWNUM <= 10 in the WHERE clause, but ROWNUM gets assigned before any ORDER BY sorting happens, so if I actually want the top 10 by price, I have to wrap the sorted query in a subquery first and filter ROWNUM on the outside, otherwise I just get an arbitrary 10 rows that happen to sort first by price after the fact. When I need something portable across more than one of these systems, I reach for the ANSI OFFSET/FETCH syntax instead, since both T-SQL and Postgres support it and it reads the same way everywhere, which matters a lot when a company's stack spans more than one database platform.
questions.example:
-- ANSI-standard, portable across T-SQL and Postgres
SELECT Name, ListPrice FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY;
commonMistakes: Assuming TOP, LIMIT, or ROWNUM syntax is universal across all SQL platforms
Filtering on Oracle's ROWNUM without realizing it's assigned before ORDER BY sorts the rows
Forgetting LIMIT needs an explicit ORDER BY to be meaningful, otherwise which rows come back is not guaranteed
Not knowing the ANSI OFFSET/FETCH syntax exists as the portable option across multiple platforms
keyPoints: T-SQL: TOP (n); MySQL/Postgres: LIMIT n [OFFSET n]
Oracle: legacy ROWNUM (assigned pre-sort) or modern FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY
ANSI-standard OFFSET/FETCH is supported by both T-SQL and Postgres for portability
Mismatched assumptions about syntax are a common source of migration bugs across platforms

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states the syntax for at least three platforms
Correctly explains the Oracle ROWNUM pre-sort quirk
Mentions the ANSI OFFSET/FETCH portable option

questions.title: Write a CASE-based price tier query
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against Production.Product that returns each product's Name, ListPrice, and a new column called PriceTier that labels products as 'Not for Sale' when ListPrice is 0, 'Budget' when ListPrice is under 100, 'Mid-Range' when it's 100 to 499.99, and 'Premium' otherwise.
questions.modelAnswer: This calls for a searched CASE expression because the conditions are ranges, not equality checks against a single value. Branch order matters: the 0 check and the under-100 check must come before the broader 100-to-499.99 check, otherwise a $0 product would never reach the 'Not for Sale' branch if a looser condition above it already matched. An ELSE catches anything at or above 500, which doubles as 'Premium' and as a safety net so no row is left with an unexpected NULL.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this as one searched CASE expression with the branches ordered from most specific to least, since CASE stops at the first true condition. The $0 check has to come first, since a product that isn't for sale at all shouldn't accidentally land in 'Budget' just because 0 is technically under 100. After that it's just a sequence of range checks, and I finish with an ELSE for 'Premium' so I'm not relying on an explicit upper bound that I'd have to remember to update if prices ever change.
questions.example:
SELECT Name, ListPrice,
  CASE WHEN ListPrice = 0 THEN 'Not for Sale'
       WHEN ListPrice < 100 THEN 'Budget'
       WHEN ListPrice < 500 THEN 'Mid-Range'
       ELSE 'Premium' END AS PriceTier
FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice;
commonMistakes: Ordering the branches so a broader condition shadows the 'Not for Sale' check
Using the simple CASE form, which can't express range conditions like ListPrice < 100
Forgetting an ELSE and leaving the highest-priced products with a NULL tier
Writing overlapping, non-exclusive conditions that make the result depend on branch order in a confusing way
keyPoints: Searched CASE is required for range-based conditions
Order branches from most specific to least specific
CASE evaluates top to bottom and stops at the first true branch
ELSE both defines the open-ended top tier and prevents unexpected NULLs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct searched CASE syntax
Branches correctly ordered to avoid shadowing
Includes ELSE and handles the boundary values correctly

questions.title: Write a COALESCE-based reporting query
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against Sales.SalesOrderHeader that returns SalesOrderID and a DeliveryLabel column, using COALESCE to show ShipDate if it exists, otherwise 'Not Yet Shipped', formatted as text.
questions.modelAnswer: COALESCE needs its arguments to share a compatible data type, and ShipDate is a datetime while 'Not Yet Shipped' is a string literal, so ShipDate has to be explicitly converted to a character type first (CONVERT or CAST) before combining them in the same COALESCE call -- otherwise SQL Server will attempt an implicit conversion of the string into a datetime and throw a conversion error. Once both arguments are the same type, COALESCE simply returns the first non-NULL value, which here means the formatted ship date whenever one exists, and the fallback text whenever ShipDate is NULL.
questions.professionalAnswer: The part I'd be careful about here isn't COALESCE itself, it's the data type mismatch -- ShipDate is a datetime and my fallback is a plain string, and COALESCE needs both sides to resolve to a compatible type. If I just write COALESCE(ShipDate, 'Not Yet Shipped') without converting ShipDate first, SQL Server tries to implicitly convert my string into a datetime, which obviously fails since 'Not Yet Shipped' isn't a valid date. So I convert ShipDate to varchar explicitly first, and then COALESCE just picks whichever one isn't NULL.
commonMistakes: Mixing a datetime and a string literal in COALESCE without converting first, causing a conversion error
Assuming COALESCE automatically formats a date the way you want rather than just returning it as-is
Using ISNULL instead and hitting the same type-mismatch issue since it has the same requirement
Forgetting COALESCE returns the data type with the highest precedence among its arguments once types are compatible
keyPoints: COALESCE requires compatible data types across all arguments
A datetime and a string literal must be explicitly converted before combining
COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument once types line up
CONVERT/CAST should happen before, not instead of, the COALESCE logic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly converts ShipDate to a compatible type
Correct COALESCE usage and syntax
Explains why the conversion is necessary

questions.title: Write a LAG-based period comparison
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query that uses the LAG() window function to show each month's total sales next to the previous month's total sales, from a table MonthlySales(SalesMonth date, TotalSales money).
questions.modelAnswer: LAG(column, offset) OVER (ORDER BY ...) looks backward a specified number of rows (1, by default) within the ordering defined inside OVER, and returns that earlier row's value alongside the current row -- without needing a self-join. Because there's no PARTITION BY needed here (there's only one sales total per month, not per group), ORDER BY SalesMonth alone defines which row is 'previous.' The first row in the ordered set has no prior row to look back to, so LAG returns NULL there by default, which is expected and should be left as NULL or explicitly handled with a default second argument rather than treated as an error.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for LAG specifically because it avoids a self-join -- the old-school way to get 'previous month' in the same row would be joining the table to itself on month minus one, which gets awkward fast. LAG(TotalSales) OVER (ORDER BY SalesMonth) just looks one row back in the ordering I specify and hands me that value directly. The one thing I always flag is that the very first month in the dataset has nothing before it, so LAG returns NULL there, which is correct behavior, not a bug -- I wouldn't want to accidentally filter that row out or treat the NULL as zero when calculating a month-over-month change.
questions.example:
SELECT SalesMonth, TotalSales,
  LAG(TotalSales) OVER (ORDER BY SalesMonth) AS PriorMonthSales,
  TotalSales - LAG(TotalSales) OVER (ORDER BY SalesMonth) AS MoMChange
FROM MonthlySales
ORDER BY SalesMonth;
commonMistakes: Reaching for a self-join instead of LAG() when a built-in window function does the job more simply
Forgetting the first row's LAG value is NULL and treating that as an error instead of expected behavior
Adding an unnecessary PARTITION BY when there's no actual grouping dimension in the data
Mixing up LAG (looks backward) with LEAD (looks forward)
keyPoints: LAG() looks backward N rows within an OVER(ORDER BY ...) window, avoiding a self-join
PARTITION BY is only needed when comparing within groups, not across the whole result
The first row in the ordering has no prior row, so LAG returns NULL there by default
LEAD() is the mirror function, looking forward instead of backward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct LAG() syntax and ORDER BY usage
Correctly computes the month-over-month change
Explains the first-row NULL behavior correctly

questions.title: Write a CTE to simplify a multi-step calculation
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query using a CTE that first computes each ProductSubcategoryID's average ListPrice, then returns only the subcategories whose average price is above the overall average across all subcategories.
questions.modelAnswer: This needs two levels of aggregation: the per-subcategory average, and then the overall average of those per-subcategory averages, compared back against each one. A CTE makes this far more readable than nesting subqueries, because the per-subcategory averages can be named once (SubcategoryAverages) and then referenced twice in the outer query -- once directly and once inside a scalar subquery computing the overall average across all rows of the CTE itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this with one CTE that computes AVG(ListPrice) grouped by ProductSubcategoryID, and then write the outer query against that CTE, comparing each subcategory's average against the overall average of all the CTE's rows -- which I get by wrapping another AVG() around a SELECT from the same CTE. Doing this without a CTE would mean nesting that same GROUP BY logic inside two separate subqueries, which works but reads much less clearly than giving the intermediate result a name once.
questions.example:
WITH SubcategoryAverages AS (
  SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, AVG(ListPrice) AS AvgPrice
  FROM Production.Product
  WHERE ProductSubcategoryID IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID
)
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, AvgPrice
FROM SubcategoryAverages
WHERE AvgPrice > (SELECT AVG(AvgPrice) FROM SubcategoryAverages);
commonMistakes: Trying to compute the overall average directly from Production.Product instead of from the per-subcategory CTE, producing a different (row-weighted) number
Forgetting to filter out NULL subcategory IDs before grouping
Nesting the logic in subqueries instead of a CTE, making the query much harder to read
Referencing the CTE's aggregated column (AvgPrice) incorrectly as if it were a raw ListPrice value
keyPoints: A CTE can be referenced more than once in the statement that follows it
Two levels of aggregation are needed: per-group, then across the groups
The overall average must be computed from the CTE's grouped results, not the raw table
CTEs improve readability over nested nested subqueries for multi-step logic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct CTE structure with per-subcategory aggregation
Correctly computes the overall average from the CTE, not the raw table
Clean, readable query structure

questions.title: Write a SUMX-based DAX measure
questions.prompt: Write a DAX measure called 'Total Line Revenue' that correctly calculates revenue as the sum of (Quantity * UnitPrice) per row in a Sales table, and explain why a naive SUM(Sales[Quantity]) * SUM(Sales[UnitPrice]) would give the wrong answer.
questions.modelAnswer: SUMX is an iterator function: it walks row by row through the table given as its first argument, evaluates the expression in its second argument once per row, and then sums all of those per-row results together -- so SUMX(Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]) correctly multiplies each row's own quantity by that same row's own unit price, then adds up those row-level products. SUM(Sales[Quantity]) * SUM(Sales[UnitPrice]) does something entirely different: it first adds up every quantity in the whole table, separately adds up every unit price in the whole table, and only then multiplies those two already-summed totals together -- which mathematically is not the same as summing the per-row products, and will produce an inflated, meaningless number as soon as rows have different quantities and prices.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write Total Line Revenue = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]), because SUMX goes row by row, multiplies quantity by price within that same row, and only sums those row-level results at the end. The naive version, SUM(Quantity) * SUM(UnitPrice), is a classic trap -- it adds up all the quantities first, adds up all the prices separately, and multiplies those two totals, which is a completely different number mathematically unless every row happens to have the exact same price. I've seen this exact mistake produce a revenue number that's wildly inflated and nobody notices until someone cross-checks it against the source system.
questions.example:
Total Line Revenue = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice])
-- 2 rows: Qty=2,Price=10 and Qty=3,Price=20
-- SUMX: (2*10) + (3*20) = 20 + 60 = 80 (correct)
-- SUM(Qty)*SUM(Price): (2+3) * (10+20) = 5 * 30 = 150 (wrong)
commonMistakes: Writing SUM(Quantity) * SUM(UnitPrice) and not noticing it's mathematically different from a per-row product sum
Not recognizing SUMX as an iterator that evaluates its expression once per row
Forgetting SUMX's first argument is the table to iterate over, not the column to sum
Assuming the error only shows up with very different row values, when it actually appears any time rows aren't all identical
keyPoints: SUMX iterates row by row, evaluating an expression per row before summing
The expression should reference row-level columns, like Quantity * UnitPrice
SUM(A) * SUM(B) is not the same as summing A*B per row
The error is invisible in the formula bar -- it only shows up as a wrong number

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct SUMX syntax
Correctly explains why the naive SUM*SUM version is wrong
Worked numeric example demonstrates the difference

questions.title: Building a one-to-many relationship in Power BI
questions.prompt: Walk through the steps you'd take in Power BI Desktop to correctly build a relationship between a Product dimension table and a Sales fact table, and how you'd verify the cardinality came out right.
questions.modelAnswer: In Model view, I'd drag from Sales[ProductID] to Product[ProductID] (or let Power BI auto-detect the relationship on load, then verify it) to create the join. Power BI inspects both columns and should automatically mark Product[ProductID] as the 'one' side, since it contains unique values, and Sales[ProductID] as the 'many' side, since the same product repeats across many sales rows. I'd then double-click the relationship line to open its properties and confirm the cardinality shows One to Many with Product on the one side, the cross-filter direction is set to single (flowing from Product to Sales) unless there's a specific reason to need both directions, and that the relationship is marked active. As a sanity check, I'd drop ProductID from Product next to a measure like SUM(Sales[LineTotal]) in a table visual and confirm the totals make sense and that filtering by a product actually filters the sales table, which confirms the relationship is wired correctly and in the right direction.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start in Model view and either let Power BI's autodetect create the relationship when I first load both tables, or drag ProductID from Sales onto ProductID in Product myself. Either way, I don't just trust it silently -- I double-click the line it creates and check three things: that Product is on the 'one' side and Sales on the 'many' side, that the cross-filter direction is single unless I have a specific reason for bidirectional, and that it's marked active rather than inactive. Then I do a quick visual sanity check -- drop Product[Name] and a sales total measure into a table and make sure the numbers look reasonable and that clicking a single product in a slicer actually filters the sales rows down, which tells me the relationship is both correctly typed and pointing the direction I expect.
commonMistakes: Trusting autodetected relationships without opening them to verify cardinality and direction
Setting cross-filter direction to bidirectional by default instead of only when there's a real need
Not noticing when Power BI creates the relationship as many-to-many due to duplicate values on both sides
Skipping a visual sanity check and only verifying the relationship exists, not that it behaves correctly
keyPoints: Build the relationship by matching the shared key column between tables
Verify which side is 'one' and which is 'many' rather than assuming
Default cross-filter direction to single unless bidirectional is specifically needed
Confirm behavior with a visual sanity check, not just by inspecting the relationship properties

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes correct steps to build the relationship
Describes how to verify cardinality and direction
Includes a practical sanity check

questions.title: Write a Tableau calculated field for profit ratio
questions.prompt: Write the Tableau calculated field formula for 'Profit Ratio' (Profit divided by Sales), and explain how you'd guard it against a divide-by-zero error when Sales is 0 for a given mark.
questions.modelAnswer: A straightforward calculated field would be SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]), aggregating both measures before dividing so the ratio is computed at whatever level of detail the view is currently showing, rather than per unaggregated row. To guard against a zero in the denominator, Tableau's IFNULL/ZN functions aren't quite right here since the issue is division by zero, not a NULL value -- the correct guard is an IF/THEN check: IF SUM([Sales]) = 0 THEN NULL ELSE SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) END, which returns NULL (which Tableau will simply leave blank or omit, depending on the visual) instead of erroring out or displaying an uninterpretable infinite value.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write it as SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]), making sure both sides are aggregated so the ratio respects whatever level of detail the current view is at, rather than trying to divide two unaggregated row-level values. For the zero-denominator case, I wrap the whole thing in an IF check: IF SUM([Sales]) = 0 THEN NULL ELSE SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) END. I specifically return NULL rather than 0 in that case, because a 0% profit ratio and 'there's no sales data to compute a ratio from' are two very different things, and silently returning 0 would make a no-data situation look like a 0% margin.
questions.example:
Profit Ratio:
IF SUM([Sales]) = 0 THEN NULL
ELSE SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales])
END

Not guarding against a zero denominator at all, risking a divide-by-zero error or null/infinite display
Returning 0 instead of NULL for the zero-sales case, misrepresenting 'no data' as a real 0% ratio
Forgetting the calculation needs to respect the current level of detail in the view, not a fixed grain
keyPoints: Aggregate both measures (SUM) before dividing so the ratio matches the view's level of detail
Guard the denominator explicitly with an IF/THEN check for zero
Return NULL rather than 0 when there's genuinely no sales to compute a ratio from
The guard belongs in the calculated field itself, not left to chance in every worksheet that uses it

Correctly guards against division by zero

questions.title: Describe building a basic ADF Copy activity pipeline
questions.prompt: Walk through the steps to build an Azure Data Factory pipeline that copies a CSV file from Azure Blob Storage into a table in Azure SQL Database using a Copy activity.
questions.modelAnswer: First, create a linked service to the Blob Storage account and a second linked service to the Azure SQL Database, ideally authenticating with a managed identity or a Key Vault-stored secret rather than a plaintext connection string. Next, create a source dataset pointing at the specific container/file path in Blob Storage, and a sink dataset pointing at the destination table in Azure SQL. Then add a Copy activity to a new pipeline, set its source to the Blob dataset (configuring the file format, such as delimited text with the correct delimiter and header settings) and its sink to the SQL dataset, and map the source columns to the destination columns, either automatically by matching names or manually if they differ. Before publishing, I'd use Data Factory's Debug run to test the pipeline against a sample file, check the activity output for rows read/written and any skipped rows, and then publish and optionally add a trigger (schedule or event-based, firing when a new file lands in the container) once the one-off test run succeeds.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set up both linked services first -- one to Blob Storage, one to the Azure SQL Database -- using managed identity or Key Vault rather than typing a password into a connection string. Then I build a source dataset pointing at the actual blob file or folder, and a sink dataset pointing at the destination table, and drop a Copy activity into a pipeline connecting the two. The part I pay the most attention to is the column mapping -- I check that source and destination columns line up correctly, especially if the CSV's column order or headers don't exactly match the table schema. Before I trust this pipeline with real data, I always run it in debug mode against a small sample file first and check the activity's output for the row counts and any errors, and only after that passes do I publish it and, if it needs to run automatically, add an event trigger so it fires whenever a new file lands in the container.

Not verifying column mapping between source and sink, causing silent data misalignment
Skipping a debug run and publishing a pipeline straight to production untested
Forgetting to configure the source dataset's file format details (delimiter, header row) correctly for the actual CSV

Create source and sink datasets pointing at the specific file and table
Add a Copy activity, configure source format and column mapping
Debug-run before publishing, then add a trigger if automation is needed

questions.title: Write a Snowflake COPY INTO statement
questions.prompt: Write a Snowflake COPY INTO statement that loads all CSV files from an internal stage called my_stage into a table called raw_orders, skipping the header row, and explain what happens if you run the exact same COPY INTO statement a second time without any new files added.
questions.code:
-- Table: raw_orders already created matching the CSV's column structure
-- Stage: @my_stage already holds uploaded CSV files
questions.modelAnswer: COPY INTO raw_orders FROM @my_stage FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = CSV SKIP_HEADER = 1); loads every file sitting in the stage into raw_orders, skipping the first row of each file as a header. Snowflake tracks, per stage, which specific files it has already successfully loaded (by file name and a checksum), so running the exact same COPY INTO statement again with no new files added will load nothing -- Snowflake recognizes those files were already loaded and skips them by default, rather than re-loading and duplicating every row. This load-history tracking is what makes COPY INTO safe to re-run as part of a scheduled or retried job without manually managing which files have or haven't been processed yet, though it can be overridden with FORCE = TRUE if a genuine reload is intentionally needed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write COPY INTO raw_orders FROM @my_stage FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = CSV SKIP_HEADER = 1);. The behavior I'd specifically call out is what happens on a re-run: Snowflake keeps track of exactly which files in that stage it already loaded, by filename and checksum, so if I run this same statement again and no new files have shown up, it loads zero rows -- it's not going to duplicate data just because I ran the command twice. That's actually really convenient for scheduled jobs, since I don't have to build my own logic to track which files have already been processed; Snowflake already does that for me. If I genuinely need to force a reload of a file that's already been loaded, I'd add FORCE = TRUE, but I wouldn't do that by default.
commonMistakes: Forgetting SKIP_HEADER = 1, loading the header row as if it were data
Assuming re-running COPY INTO will duplicate already-loaded rows instead of being skipped automatically
Not knowing FORCE = TRUE exists to intentionally override the default skip-already-loaded behavior
Confusing an internal stage (Snowflake-managed storage) with an external stage (a cloud storage bucket you manage)
keyPoints: COPY INTO loads staged files into a target table with a specified file format
Snowflake tracks which files were already successfully loaded per stage
Re-running COPY INTO with no new files loads nothing by default, avoiding duplicates
FORCE = TRUE can override that default when an intentional reload is needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct COPY INTO syntax including SKIP_HEADER
Correctly explains the file-tracking/no-duplicate-load behavior
Mentions FORCE = TRUE as the override

questions.title: Write a basic dbt staging model
questions.prompt: Write a simple dbt staging model (stg_customers.sql) that selects and renames a few raw columns from a source table, using source() rather than ref() or a hardcoded table name, and explain why a staging model like this typically shouldn't contain business logic like joins or aggregations.
questions.code:
-- sources.yml declares: source 'raw', table 'customers'
-- raw.customers columns: cust_id, cust_fname, cust_lname, cust_email_addr
questions.modelAnswer: A staging model's job is narrow and deliberate: rename cryptic raw column names into clean, consistent ones, cast data types if needed, and otherwise pass the data through mostly unchanged -- one staging model per raw source table, referenced through source(), which (like ref() for other dbt models) lets dbt track it as a declared dependency and resolve the correct physical table name per environment. Staging models avoid joins, aggregations, or business logic specifically so that every downstream model built on top of them is working from a clean, predictable, one-to-one representation of the raw data -- pushing that complexity down into staging models instead would make it much harder to trace where a join or a business rule actually lives when something downstream needs debugging, and would duplicate that logic across every staging model that happened to need it instead of keeping it in one shared intermediate or mart-level model.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep this model intentionally boring -- just select the raw columns from source('raw', 'customers'), rename them to something clean and consistent like customer_id and first_name, and stop there. The reason I don't add a join or an aggregation here is about where logic should live: if every staging model does its own ad hoc business logic, that logic gets duplicated and scattered everywhere, and when a number looks wrong two layers downstream, I have no idea which staging model to even start checking. Keeping staging models as a thin, consistent renaming layer means I always know exactly where to look for real business logic -- it lives in the intermediate or mart layer, not here.
questions.example:
-- models/staging/stg_customers.sql
SELECT
  cust_id AS customer_id,
  cust_fname AS first_name,
  cust_lname AS last_name,
  cust_email_addr AS email
FROM {{ source('raw', 'customers') }}
commonMistakes: Hardcoding the raw table name instead of using source(), losing dbt's dependency tracking and lineage
Adding a join or aggregation into a staging model instead of keeping it a thin renaming layer
Not giving columns clean, consistent names, leaving cryptic raw names to propagate downstream
Confusing source() (for raw tables dbt didn't build) with ref() (for other dbt models)
keyPoints: Staging models use source() to reference raw tables, preserving dbt's dependency tracking
Staging models rename/cast columns but avoid joins, aggregations, and business logic
Keeping staging thin makes it easy to know where real business logic lives downstream
One staging model typically maps to one raw source table

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct use of source() rather than hardcoding or ref()
Correct, clean column renaming
Explains why business logic doesn't belong in staging

questions.title: Write a PIVOT query
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query using PIVOT that turns rows of (Color, ListPrice) from Production.Product into a single result with one column per color, showing the average ListPrice for each color.
questions.modelAnswer: PIVOT turns distinct values from one column into separate output columns, aggregating another column's values into each one. The syntax requires wrapping the source query in a derived table that includes only the columns actually needed (Color and ListPrice here), then specifying the aggregate function to apply (AVG), the column whose values become new columns (Color), and the explicit list of values to pivot into columns, written out by hand since PIVOT doesn't dynamically discover distinct values on its own -- any color not listed in that IN() clause is silently excluded from the result rather than causing an error.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build the inner query first, selecting just Color and ListPrice, since PIVOT only works cleanly against the specific columns it needs. Then the PIVOT clause itself names AVG(ListPrice) as the aggregation, Color as the column to spread out, and an explicit list of the actual color values in IN(). The thing I'd flag as a gotcha is that this list has to be hand-typed -- if a new color gets added to the product catalog later and I don't update the IN() list, that color just silently disappears from the pivoted result instead of throwing any kind of warning, which is why PIVOT works best for a known, stable set of categories rather than something that changes often.

Not restricting the inner query to only the needed columns before pivoting
Expecting a color left out of the IN() list to cause an error instead of being silently dropped
Trying to pivot on a column with too many distinct values, producing an unreasonably wide result

Requires an inner query restricted to only the relevant columns
The list of values to pivot must be explicitly specified, not auto-discovered
Values not included in the list are silently excluded from the result

Correct aggregate function and pivot column choice
