questions.title: Write a stored procedure with TRY/CATCH
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL stored procedure that inserts a new row into a Products table and uses TRY/CATCH to handle any error gracefully, returning the error message instead of letting the batch fail silently or crash the caller.
questions.code: -- Products(ProductID int PK, Name nvarchar(50), ListPrice money)
questions.modelAnswer: BEGIN TRY wraps the risky statement (here, the INSERT, which could fail on a primary key violation, a type mismatch, or a constraint violation); if it throws, control jumps to the matching BEGIN CATCH block instead of letting the error propagate uncaught. Inside CATCH, the built-in functions ERROR_MESSAGE(), ERROR_NUMBER(), and ERROR_SEVERITY() capture details about exactly what went wrong, which can be returned to the caller, logged, or re-thrown with THROW if the procedure shouldn't swallow the error entirely. This pattern matters because without it, an unhandled error in a stored procedure can leave the caller with a cryptic failure and no useful diagnostic information, or in some cases leave a transaction in an inconsistent state if multiple statements were involved.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd wrap the INSERT in BEGIN TRY / END TRY, and in the matching BEGIN CATCH / END CATCH block, capture ERROR_MESSAGE() and ERROR_NUMBER() and return them to the caller instead of letting the error just bubble up as a raw SQL Server exception. That gives whoever's calling this procedure something actually useful to look at instead of a generic failure. If this insert were part of a larger multi-statement transaction, I'd also make sure to roll that transaction back inside the CATCH block before returning, since an error partway through a transaction can otherwise leave data in a half-finished state.
commonMistakes: Not wrapping risky statements in TRY/CATCH at all, letting an error crash the caller with no diagnostic detail
Catching the error but not surfacing ERROR_MESSAGE()/ERROR_NUMBER() to the caller in any useful way
Forgetting to roll back a transaction inside CATCH when the failed statement was part of a multi-step transaction
Using CATCH to silently swallow every error instead of distinguishing errors worth surfacing from ones genuinely safe to ignore
keyPoints: BEGIN TRY wraps the statement(s) that might fail
BEGIN CATCH captures control on failure instead of letting the error propagate uncaught
ERROR_MESSAGE()/ERROR_NUMBER() provide diagnostic detail inside CATCH
A transaction should be rolled back inside CATCH if the failure occurred mid-transaction

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct TRY/CATCH syntax
Correctly surfaces error detail to the caller
Mentions transaction rollback consideration

questions.title: Troubleshooting a join fan-out inflating totals
questions.prompt: A report's total revenue is showing almost double the correct number after you added a join to bring in shipping details. How would you diagnose and fix a join that's unexpectedly multiplying rows (a 'fan-out')?
questions.modelAnswer: A fan-out happens when the newly joined table has more than one matching row per row on the other side -- here, if a single order has multiple shipping-detail rows (say, a package split into two shipments), joining Orders to Shipping duplicates that order's revenue once for every matching shipping row, and summing after the join counts that same revenue multiple times. The fix is to figure out the actual grain mismatch: either aggregate the shipping table down to one row per order before joining (e.g., summing shipment count but not revenue, or picking just the most recent shipment), or move the shipping detail into a separate query entirely rather than joining it at the same grain as the revenue calculation. The general diagnostic step is to count rows before and after adding the join -- if the row count jumped without a corresponding real increase in the underlying order count, that's the fan-out revealing itself immediately.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is whether the row count changed when I added that join -- if orders went from, say, 10,000 rows to 15,000 rows after joining shipping details, that's the tell that shipping has more than one row per order, and every extra matching row is duplicating that order's revenue in the sum. Once I confirm that's the cause, I have a choice: either pre-aggregate the shipping table down to one row per order before joining it (if I just need something like a shipment count, not a sum that compounds the duplication), or pull the shipping detail into a completely separate query so I'm not joining two different grains together in the same SUM. I'd never just add a DISTINCT to paper over it, since that can hide real duplicate orders along with the fan-out duplicates and isn't addressing the actual grain mismatch.
commonMistakes: Adding DISTINCT to 'fix' the symptom instead of addressing the underlying grain mismatch
Not checking row counts before and after adding a join to catch a fan-out early
Assuming every join to a 'detail' table is safe without checking whether it's actually one-to-many
Fixing the fan-out for one measure but leaving other aggregates in the same query still inflated
keyPoints: A fan-out occurs when a join brings in more than one matching row per original row
Summing after a fan-out double- or multi-counts the original row's values
Checking row counts before/after a join reveals the fan-out quickly
Fix by pre-aggregating to the correct grain or separating the queries, not by bolting on DISTINCT

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the fan-out mechanism
Describes a real diagnostic step (row count check)
Proposes a correct fix, not a superficial workaround

questions.title: Troubleshooting inflated totals from a many-to-many relationship
questions.prompt: A Power BI report's total sales number is inflated after a new dimension table was added to the model. You suspect the relationship between it and the fact table is many-to-many instead of one-to-many. How would you confirm that and fix the model?
questions.modelAnswer: First, I'd open Model view and check the relationship line's cardinality indicator -- Power BI marks a many-to-many relationship distinctly from one-to-many. If it's showing many-to-many, that means the column used for the relationship contains duplicate values on both sides, not just the fact table side, which is the actual root cause. Many-to-many relationships behave differently under the hood: without a true shared, unique key on at least one side, filter propagation becomes ambiguous and can effectively multiply matching rows together, inflating aggregated totals. The real fix is almost always to introduce a proper bridge or lookup table containing the unique key values, turning what was one many-to-many relationship into two clean one-to-many relationships -- fact-to-bridge and dimension-to-bridge -- rather than leaving the model with an ambiguous many-to-many join.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go straight to Model view and look at the relationship's cardinality marker, since Power BI will tell me directly if it created a many-to-many relationship instead of one-to-many. If that's what happened, it almost always means the column I used for the join has duplicates on both sides, not a clean unique key on either one. Rather than just leaving that many-to-many relationship in place and hoping the numbers work out, I'd build a small bridge table that has the unique key values exactly once, and reconnect both the fact table and the dimension table to that bridge instead of to each other directly -- that turns one ambiguous many-to-many relationship into two clean one-to-many relationships, which is what actually fixes the inflated totals rather than just hiding the symptom.
commonMistakes: Not checking the relationship cardinality indicator in Model view before assuming the cause
Leaving a many-to-many relationship in place and trying to fix the inflated numbers with DAX instead of the model structure
Not recognizing that a many-to-many relationship means duplicates exist on both sides, not just one
Building a bridge table but forgetting to make its key column actually unique
keyPoints: Check the relationship's cardinality in Model view to confirm many-to-many
Many-to-many means duplicate values exist on both sides of the join column
A many-to-many relationship can make filter propagation ambiguous and inflate totals
The standard fix is a bridge table creating two clean one-to-many relationships

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies how to confirm many-to-many cardinality
Correctly explains why it inflates totals
Proposes the bridge table fix correctly

questions.title: Troubleshooting an ADF pipeline authentication failure
questions.prompt: An Azure Data Factory pipeline that's been running fine for months suddenly starts failing every run with an authentication error against the source database. How would you investigate and resolve it?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start in the ADF monitoring pane, open the failed run, and read the actual error message on the failing activity rather than guessing -- authentication failures usually come with a specific error code (expired credential, locked account, access revoked) that narrows the cause immediately. The most common culprits for a pipeline that 'suddenly' breaks after working fine are a password or secret that expired or was rotated in the source system without updating the linked service, a managed identity that lost a role assignment (someone cleaned up permissions elsewhere), or a firewall/network rule change on the source database blocking the integration runtime's IP. I'd check the linked service's connection test directly from the ADF authoring UI, verify whether the credential is a Key Vault reference (and if so, check whether that secret itself expired or was rotated in the vault, not just in ADF), and confirm the identity or account still has the correct role assignment on the source resource.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't guess -- I'd open the monitoring view, find the failed activity, and read the actual error text, since Data Factory is usually specific about whether it's an expired credential, a blocked network path, or a missing permission. Given it was working for months and suddenly broke, my first suspicion is something changed on the source side rather than in ADF itself -- a rotated password, an expired Key Vault secret, or a managed identity that lost a role assignment during some unrelated cleanup. I'd test the linked service's connection directly from the ADF UI to isolate whether it's a connectivity problem or an authentication problem specifically, and if it's using Key Vault, I'd check the secret's expiration and version in the vault itself, not just assume ADF's reference to it is still valid.
commonMistakes: Re-running the pipeline repeatedly without reading the actual error message first
Assuming the problem is in ADF itself instead of checking whether something changed on the source system
Not testing the linked service connection directly to isolate authentication from network connectivity
Overlooking that a Key Vault-referenced secret can itself expire or rotate independently of the ADF configuration
keyPoints: Start with the actual error message on the failed activity in the monitoring pane
Consider expired/rotated credentials, lost role assignments, and network/firewall changes
Test the linked service connection directly to isolate authentication from other failure types
Check Key Vault secret validity separately from the ADF linked service configuration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Starts diagnosis from the actual error message, not guessing
Identifies plausible real causes (credential rotation, role loss, firewall)
Describes a concrete verification step

questions.title: Troubleshooting a slow Snowflake query
questions.prompt: A dashboard query against Snowflake that used to run in a few seconds is now taking several minutes. What would you check first, and what are the most common beginner-level causes?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by checking the Query Profile in Snowflake's history/monitoring view for that specific query run, which shows where time was actually spent -- scanning data, waiting on a queue, or something else. The most common beginner-level causes are: the virtual warehouse is undersized for the amount of data now being scanned (data volume grew since the query was first written, but the warehouse size never changed), the warehouse was suspended and the first query after a resume pays a brief cold-start cost, the warehouse is being shared by other heavy workloads at the same time and the query is waiting in a queue rather than actually running slowly, or a result-cache hit that used to make the query feel instant stopped applying because the underlying data changed. I'd also check whether the query is scanning far more partitions than it needs to -- a missing or ineffective filter on a large table, now that the table has grown, can mean a query that used to scan a small amount of data is now scanning a much larger one.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd pull up is the Query Profile for that specific run, since it tells me exactly where the time went instead of me guessing. A few things I'd specifically rule in or out: has the underlying table grown a lot since this query was first written, meaning the same filter now scans way more data; is the warehouse sized appropriately for that volume, or did it stay small while the data grew; is the warehouse being hammered by other jobs at the same time, so some of that 'slowness' is actually queueing, not query execution; and was this query previously benefiting from Snowflake's result cache, which stops helping the moment the underlying data changes. I wouldn't jump straight to resizing the warehouse bigger as the fix -- that costs more money, and if the real issue is a missing filter or a queueing problem, a bigger warehouse won't necessarily solve it.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to resizing the warehouse bigger without checking the Query Profile first
Not considering that query queueing from other concurrent workloads can look like slowness
Forgetting that a previously cache-hit query stops benefiting once the underlying data changes
Not checking whether the underlying table has simply grown since the query was first written
keyPoints: Start with the Query Profile to see where time is actually spent
Check for data volume growth against a warehouse size that hasn't changed
Consider queueing from concurrent workloads on the same warehouse
Consider loss of result-cache benefit if underlying data changed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Starts with the Query Profile rather than guessing
Identifies plausible real causes
Avoids jumping straight to 'just make the warehouse bigger'

questions.title: Troubleshooting a failing dbt test
questions.prompt: A dbt run completes successfully, but a unique test on a model's primary key column starts failing. Walk through how you'd investigate and what a beginner should check first.
questions.modelAnswer: A dbt run and a dbt test are separate steps -- the run can succeed (the model built without a SQL error) while the test still fails, because tests check the resulting data's quality, not whether the SQL executed. I'd start by running dbt test --select <model_name> to confirm exactly which test failed and look at the generated query dbt ran to check uniqueness -- dbt stores a compiled SQL file for every test that I can open and run manually to see the actual duplicate rows. The most common beginner causes are an upstream source that introduced a genuine duplicate (a source system sent the same record twice), a join earlier in the model's logic fanning out and producing more than one row per key, or a key that was never actually guaranteed unique by the source system in the first place, meaning the test's assumption was wrong from the start, not the data. I'd look at the actual duplicate rows the compiled test query returns before guessing at a fix, since the right fix depends entirely on which of these it turns out to be.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd remind myself is that a successful dbt run and a passing dbt test are two different things -- the model can build fine and the test can still catch a real data quality problem. I'd run dbt test --select that model specifically, then go find the compiled SQL dbt generated for that test, which I can run directly to see the actual duplicate key values rather than just knowing the test failed. From there it usually comes down to one of three things: a genuine duplicate showed up upstream in the source, a join inside the model is fanning out rows, or the key was never truly unique to begin with and the test's assumption needs to change rather than the model. I always look at the real duplicate rows before touching any code, because fixing the wrong thing based on a guess usually just hides the symptom instead of solving it.
commonMistakes: Assuming a successful dbt run means the data is fine, without checking test results separately
Trying to fix the model's code before looking at the actual duplicate rows the test caught
Not knowing dbt generates a compiled, runnable SQL query for each test that can be inspected directly
Assuming the key itself was always guaranteed unique instead of questioning that assumption
keyPoints: A successful dbt run does not guarantee passing dbt tests
dbt test --select isolates which specific test failed
The compiled test SQL can be run directly to inspect the actual offending rows
Common root causes: upstream duplicates, a fan-out join, or a key that was never truly unique

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes a dbt run from a dbt test
Describes inspecting the actual failing rows before fixing

questions.title: Troubleshooting a T-SQL deadlock
questions.prompt: A stored procedure that normally runs fine starts intermittently failing with error 1205, a deadlock victim error. What is a deadlock, and what would you check or change to reduce how often it happens?
questions.modelAnswer: A deadlock happens when two transactions each hold a lock the other one needs, and each is waiting for the other to release it -- neither can proceed, so SQL Server detects the cycle and forcibly kills one of them (the 'deadlock victim') with error 1205 so the other can continue. Because it depends on timing and which two transactions happen to collide, it's typically intermittent rather than reproducible on demand. A practical first step is turning on trace flag 1222 or enabling the system_health extended events session to capture the deadlock graph, which shows exactly which two statements and which resources were involved. Common beginner-level fixes include making sure transactions access tables in a consistent order across all procedures that touch them (so two transactions can't lock resources in opposite orders), keeping transactions as short as possible so locks are held for less time, and adding appropriate indexes so a transaction isn't holding a broader lock than it needs to because it's scanning more rows than necessary.
questions.professionalAnswer: A deadlock is basically two transactions stuck in a standoff -- each one is holding a lock the other needs, so neither can move forward, and SQL Server eventually steps in and kills one of them to break the tie, which is exactly what error 1205 means. The fact that it's intermittent rather than constant is actually expected, since it depends on the unlucky timing of two specific transactions colliding. The first thing I'd do is capture the deadlock graph, either through the system_health extended events session or trace flag 1222, because that tells me exactly which two statements and which resources were actually involved instead of me guessing. From there, the usual fixes are making sure every procedure that touches the same set of tables accesses them in the same order, keeping transactions as short as possible so they're not holding locks longer than necessary, and checking whether a missing index is forcing a broader scan and lock than the query actually needs.
commonMistakes: Assuming a deadlock is a bug in one specific procedure rather than a timing collision between two transactions
Not capturing the deadlock graph before attempting a fix, and guessing at the cause instead
Fixing table access order in one procedure but leaving another procedure touching the same tables in a different order
Wrapping everything in a longer transaction 'to be safe' instead of keeping transactions as short as possible
keyPoints: A deadlock is a circular lock-wait between two transactions, resolved by killing one as the 'victim'
Error 1205 is intermittent because it depends on unlucky timing between two specific transactions
Capture the deadlock graph (trace flag 1222 or system_health) before guessing at a fix
Common fixes: consistent table access order, shorter transactions, appropriate indexing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a deadlock is and why 1205 occurs
Describes a concrete diagnostic step (deadlock graph)
Proposes sensible mitigation strategies

questions.title: Troubleshooting a stale Tableau extract
questions.prompt: Users are complaining that a Tableau dashboard is showing numbers from last week, even though the underlying source data is updated daily. How would you figure out why and fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Since the dashboard is behind on data that the source already has, the most likely explanation is that the workbook is connected via an extract rather than a live connection, and the scheduled refresh for that extract either failed, was never actually scheduled, or is running on a cadence (say, weekly) that doesn't match expectations (daily). I'd check Tableau Server/Cloud's extract refresh schedule and run history for that specific workbook first -- the history will show whether refreshes have been running on schedule and whether any have been failing silently, which is common if an upstream credential expired or a source table was renamed. If refreshes are running successfully but the data still looks old, I'd check whether the extract itself is an incremental refresh configured against a column that isn't actually being updated correctly, which can cause new rows to be silently skipped even though the refresh 'succeeds.'
questions.professionalAnswer: My first assumption is that this is an extract, not a live connection, since a live connection by definition can't show week-old data if the source itself is current. I'd go straight to the extract's refresh schedule and run history on Tableau Server or Cloud and check two things: is it actually scheduled to run as often as people expect, and are those scheduled runs actually succeeding, or failing silently in the background. A failed refresh due to an expired credential or a renamed source table is a really common cause, and it often fails quietly enough that nobody notices until a user flags stale numbers. If the schedule and run history both look fine, my next suspicion would be an incremental refresh that's misconfigured against the wrong date column, which can make a refresh report success while actually missing the new rows it should have picked up.
commonMistakes: Assuming the dashboard is live-connected without checking whether it's actually an extract
Not checking the extract's refresh run history, missing a silently failing scheduled refresh
Fixing the schedule's frequency without first confirming the refreshes were even succeeding
Not considering a misconfigured incremental refresh as a cause of a 'successful' refresh that still misses new data

Check the extract's scheduled refresh history for failures, not just whether a schedule exists
A refresh can fail silently due to an expired credential or renamed source object

questions.title: Troubleshooting a NULL-skewed aggregate
questions.prompt: A COUNT(DiscountCode) on an orders table returns a much smaller number than COUNT(*) on the same table, and a report built on top of it looks wrong as a result. Why does this happen, and how would you decide which one is actually correct for the report?
questions.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS AllOrders, COUNT(DiscountCode) AS OrdersWithCodeCounted
FROM Sales.Orders;
questions.modelAnswer: COUNT(*) counts every row in the table regardless of NULLs anywhere, while COUNT(<column>) counts only the rows where that specific column is not NULL -- so the gap between the two numbers is exactly the number of orders that have no discount code at all. Neither number is inherently 'wrong'; they're answering two different questions. The real fix is figuring out which question the report actually needs to answer: if the report is meant to say 'how many orders were placed in total,' COUNT(*) is correct; if it's meant to say 'how many orders actually had a discount applied,' COUNT(DiscountCode) is correct, and the smaller number is the accurate one, not a bug. The mistake worth avoiding is assuming one of the two counts must be broken just because they don't match, rather than checking which business question the report is supposed to be answering.
questions.professionalAnswer: This isn't actually a bug in either count -- COUNT(*) counts rows, period, while COUNT(DiscountCode) specifically skips any row where that column is NULL, so the difference between them is literally the number of orders with no discount code. Before I'd change anything, I'd go back to whoever's using this report and ask which question they're actually trying to answer: total order volume, or orders that specifically had a discount applied. If it's the latter, the smaller COUNT(DiscountCode) number is the right one and the report was built correctly -- there's no fix needed on the query, just a clearer label on what the metric actually represents, since 'orders' without more context is ambiguous enough to cause this exact kind of confusion.

Not checking which business question the report is actually meant to answer before changing the query
Forgetting COUNT(*) counts rows while COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values of that specific column
Mislabeling the metric in the report instead of clarifying what it actually represents

The gap between the two is exactly the count of NULLs in that column

questions.title: Choosing star vs. snowflake schema
questions.prompt: At a beginner level, what's the difference between a star schema and a snowflake schema, and why would you typically default to a star schema for a reporting data mart unless there's a specific reason not to?
questions.modelAnswer: A star schema has one central fact table surrounded directly by denormalized dimension tables -- each dimension holds all of its own descriptive attributes in one flat table, even if that means some repeated data (like repeating a category name across every product row that belongs to it). A snowflake schema takes those dimensions a step further and normalizes them into additional related sub-dimension tables -- Product might reference a separate ProductCategory table, which references a separate ProductDepartment table, and so on. Star schemas are generally preferred for reporting because they require fewer joins to get from a fact table to any given attribute, which both simplifies queries that analysts and BI tools write and typically performs better, especially in columnar/MPP warehouses that are optimized for scanning flat, wide tables rather than chasing many small joins. Snowflaking makes sense when storage efficiency genuinely matters more than query simplicity, or when a dimension's hierarchy itself needs to be modeled and maintained with strict referential integrity -- but for most BI reporting use cases, the extra joins aren't worth the storage savings, especially now that storage is cheap relative to compute.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe a star schema as the dimension tables staying flat and a little repetitive -- Product has Category right there as a column, even though that means the word 'Electronics' is physically repeated on every electronics product row. A snowflake schema takes that same Category out into its own separate table and links to it, which is more storage-efficient but means an extra join every time a query needs that category. My default for a reporting mart is star schema, because BI tools and the people writing queries against it both benefit from fewer joins, and most modern warehouses are built to scan a flat table efficiently rather than reward normalized joins the way an OLTP system would. I'd only lean toward snowflaking a dimension if there's a real reason -- like a deep, genuinely hierarchical structure that needs to be maintained with strict integrity on its own, or a storage cost concern that's actually material, which is rare enough in practice that star schema stays my default.

Forgetting storage savings from snowflaking are often negligible compared to modern storage costs

Snowflake schema: dimensions further normalized into related sub-tables

questions.title: ETL vs. ELT
questions.prompt: What's the difference between ETL and ELT, and why has ELT become the more common pattern now that cloud warehouses like Snowflake and tools like dbt are part of the standard stack?
questions.modelAnswer: ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) transforms data in a separate processing layer before it ever reaches the warehouse -- data is pulled from the source, cleaned and reshaped by an external engine, and only the finished result is loaded into the destination. ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) instead loads the raw data into the warehouse first, mostly as-is, and does the transformation afterward using the warehouse's own compute -- which is exactly the model dbt is built around, writing transformation logic as SQL models that run inside Snowflake, Databricks, or another modern warehouse rather than in a separate tool. ELT became the dominant pattern because modern cloud warehouses have cheap, elastically scalable compute that can comfortably absorb heavy transformation workloads, and keeping the raw, untransformed data available in the warehouse (rather than discarding it after an external ETL tool processes it) makes it much easier to re-run a changed transformation later or debug by going back to the original source data. ETL still has its place when a transformation has to happen before data is allowed to land anywhere, such as scrubbing sensitive fields for a compliance reason before the data is stored at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain ETL as transform-before-you-land -- the data gets reshaped outside the warehouse, by some other engine, and only the final, already-clean result actually makes it into the warehouse. ELT flips that: load the raw data in first, mostly untouched, and do the transformation afterward using the warehouse's own compute, which is literally what dbt does -- it's just SQL models running inside Snowflake or wherever the warehouse lives. The reason ELT took over is mostly that cloud warehouse compute got cheap and elastic enough that doing the transformation there isn't a burden anymore, and keeping the raw data sitting in the warehouse means if I ever need to change a transformation or debug something, I've still got the original source data to go back to instead of having thrown it away during an ETL step. I'd still reach for a true ETL approach if there were a hard requirement to scrub something sensitive before it's ever allowed to land in the warehouse at all, but that's the exception now, not the default.

Forgetting raw data retention in ELT is itself a benefit for debugging and re-running changed logic
Not recognizing legitimate cases (compliance scrubbing) where ETL is still the right call

ELT loads raw data first, then transforms it using the warehouse's own compute
ELT's rise is tied to cheap elastic cloud compute and tools like dbt
Retaining raw data in ELT makes re-running/debugging transformations easier

questions.title: OLTP vs. OLAP
questions.prompt: What's the difference between an OLTP system and an OLAP system, and why is it usually a bad idea to run heavy analytical reporting queries directly against a production OLTP database?
questions.modelAnswer: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) systems are optimized for fast, small, frequent reads and writes -- a point-of-sale system inserting one order at a time, an application updating one customer's address -- and their schema is usually highly normalized to keep those individual writes fast and consistent. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) systems are optimized for the opposite workload: large, complex queries that scan and aggregate huge volumes of historical data, usually structured with denormalized dimensional models like a star schema specifically to make that kind of scanning efficient. Running heavy analytical queries directly against a production OLTP database is risky for two reasons: the query patterns are fundamentally mismatched with what the OLTP system's indexes and schema were designed for, so those queries tend to be slow and resource-intensive, and more importantly, a long-running analytical query can hold locks or consume enough resources to actually slow down or block the live transactions the business depends on in real time -- which is exactly why a separate reporting warehouse or replica exists, so analytics and live transaction processing don't compete for the same resources.
questions.professionalAnswer: OLTP is built for lots of small, fast transactions happening constantly -- think of every individual order being placed, normalized tightly so those writes stay quick and consistent. OLAP is the opposite workload -- big, scan-heavy queries aggregating years of history, usually against a denormalized star schema built specifically for that kind of scanning. The reason I wouldn't run a heavy analytical report straight against the production OLTP database isn't just that it would be slow, though it usually is -- it's that a long-running report can hold locks or eat up resources the live application needs to keep processing real orders, which can mean actual customers experiencing a slow or broken checkout because someone's dashboard query is hogging the database. That's the whole reason a separate data warehouse or at least a read replica exists -- so reporting and live transactions aren't fighting over the same resources.
commonMistakes: Assuming the main risk of querying OLTP directly is just query speed, not impact on live transactions
Not connecting the schema difference (normalized vs. denormalized) to the workload each is optimized for
Assuming a read replica or warehouse is just a 'nice to have' rather than a real operational safeguard
Confusing OLTP's 'many small transactions' pattern with OLAP's 'few large scans' pattern
keyPoints: OLTP: fast, small, frequent transactions, normalized schema
OLAP: large, complex analytical queries, typically denormalized dimensional schema
Running analytics on production OLTP risks slowing or blocking live transactions
A separate warehouse or replica isolates reporting workload from live transaction processing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes OLTP from OLAP workloads
Explains the real operational risk of querying production OLTP directly
Mentions the standard mitigation (replica/warehouse)

questions.title: The medallion architecture (bronze, silver, gold)
questions.prompt: What is the medallion architecture used in Databricks/Delta Lake lakehouse designs, and what's the purpose of each of the bronze, silver, and gold layers?
questions.modelAnswer: The medallion architecture is a layered organization pattern for a lakehouse that progressively refines data in stages rather than transforming it all in one leap. The bronze layer holds raw data landed as close to its original source format as possible -- minimal or no transformation, kept so the original data is always available to reprocess if downstream logic needs to change or a bug is found. The silver layer applies cleaning, validation, deduplication, and conforming of types and schema across sources -- it's meant to represent a trustworthy, queryable version of the data, but not yet shaped specifically for any one business question. The gold layer applies the actual business logic -- aggregations, joins across domains, metrics calculated exactly the way a specific report or team needs them -- and is what BI tools and end users typically query directly. The value of structuring it this way is that each layer has a clear, single responsibility, a bug in business logic can be fixed by rebuilding just the gold layer from silver without needing to re-ingest raw source data, and the bronze layer's raw retention protects against ever losing the ability to reprocess data correctly after a mistake in an earlier transformation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe it as data getting progressively more refined and more purpose-built as it moves through three stages. Bronze is raw, landed pretty much exactly as it came from the source, kept that way specifically so I never lose the ability to reprocess from scratch if something downstream turns out to be wrong. Silver is where I clean things up -- dedupe, fix types, validate -- so it's a trustworthy general-purpose version of the data, but it's not yet tailored to any specific report. Gold is where the actual business logic lives -- the aggregations and metrics a specific dashboard or team actually needs -- and that's the layer BI tools point at. The real benefit of splitting it this way is isolation: if a business rule in gold turns out to be wrong, I can fix and rebuild just that layer from silver without touching bronze at all, and because bronze still has the raw data, I'm never stuck unable to go back and reprocess correctly if an earlier transformation step had a bug in it.
commonMistakes: Applying business logic directly in the bronze or silver layer instead of isolating it in gold
Not retaining raw bronze data, losing the ability to reprocess after a downstream bug
Treating silver as already business-ready instead of just clean and conformed
Skipping straight from raw to gold without a cleaning/conforming silver layer in between
keyPoints: Bronze: raw, minimally transformed data, retained for reprocessing
Silver: cleaned, validated, deduplicated, conformed, general-purpose data
Gold: business logic applied, purpose-built for specific reporting/analytics needs
Layer isolation lets a bug be fixed by rebuilding just the affected layer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the purpose of each layer
Explains the benefit of layer isolation/raw retention
Clarity of explanation

deepDive.heading: Why bronze retention is the layer people underrate
deepDive.content: New data engineers often treat bronze as just a wasteful extra copy of the data, but it's the layer that makes the whole architecture resilient. If someone discovers six months from now that a type-casting rule in the silver layer was subtly wrong for a certain date range, having bronze intact means that silver and gold can simply be rebuilt from the untouched raw data for that range -- no need to go back to the original source system, which may have already purged or changed the data by then. Delta Lake's own transaction log and time travel features complement this well: even silver and gold tables can be rolled back to an earlier version if a bad transformation was already promoted, but bronze is the real safety net when the fix requires reprocessing logic rather than just reverting to a prior table version.

questions.title: Handling ambiguous requirements from a stakeholder
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks you to 'build a dashboard showing how the sales team is doing' with no further detail. Walk me through how you'd handle that request before you start building anything.
questions.modelAnswer: A request this vague has too many possible interpretations to start building against -- 'how the sales team is doing' could mean revenue against quota, deal velocity, win rate, activity volume, or several of those together, and guessing wrong wastes real build time and erodes the stakeholder's trust that I understood the ask. I'd schedule a short conversation and ask specific, concrete questions: what decision will this dashboard inform, who's going to look at it and how often, what time grain matters (daily, monthly, quarterly), is there an existing metric definition I should match (so my 'revenue' lines up with Finance's 'revenue'), and is there a comparable report I can look at for a sense of expected shape. I'd also ask what 'good' looks like -- a target, a quota, a prior period to compare against -- since a number with no benchmark is often not actionable. Only after those answers are clear would I sketch a quick mockup or wireframe and confirm it with the stakeholder before building the real thing, which catches a misunderstanding cheaply instead of after a full build.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, my first instinct with a request this open-ended isn't to start building -- it's to ask a handful of specific questions, because 'how the sales team is doing' could mean five different things depending on who's asking and why. I'd ask what decision this is actually going to support, who's looking at it and how often, and whether there's already an agreed definition for something like 'revenue' that I need to match rather than inventing my own. I'd also specifically ask what they're comparing against -- a quota, last quarter, last year -- because a number with nothing to compare it to usually isn't that useful on its own. Once I've got clear answers, I like to sketch a rough mockup and get a thumbs-up on that before I actually build anything, since it's a lot cheaper to catch a misunderstanding on a sketch than after I've spent hours building the real dashboard.
commonMistakes: Starting to build immediately on a vague request instead of clarifying scope first
Not asking what decision the dashboard needs to support, building metrics without a clear purpose
Inventing a metric definition instead of checking whether one already exists elsewhere in the business
Skipping a mockup/sketch confirmation step and only getting feedback after a full build
keyPoints: Vague requests should be clarified before building, not guessed at
Ask what decision the output needs to support and who will use it
Check for existing metric definitions rather than inventing new ones
Confirm a mockup/sketch before committing to a full build

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes clarifying questions before building
Shows awareness of metric-definition consistency across the business
Mentions a low-cost validation step (mockup) before full build

questions.title: A report that had wrong numbers
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time (real or how you'd approach it) when a report or dashboard you built was flagged as showing incorrect numbers. How did you handle finding out, investigating, and communicating about it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats this as a process, not just an apology: first, acknowledge the issue quickly and without being defensive, since stakeholders care more about getting a fix than about whose fault it was. Second, reproduce the discrepancy concretely -- find the specific number that's wrong, trace it back through the model or query to find exactly where it diverges from the expected or source value, rather than guessing at a cause. Common root causes worth checking systematically include a join fan-out inflating a total, a filter that's excluding or including the wrong rows, a measure using the wrong aggregation (SUM where AVG was needed, or vice versa), or a timing mismatch between when the report refreshed and when the source data last updated. Third, once the cause is found, fix it, verify the fix against a known-correct number, and communicate clearly what was wrong, what was fixed, and whether any decisions were made based on the bad numbers that might need revisiting. A good answer also mentions a preventive step going forward, like adding a sanity-check total or test to catch a similar error automatically next time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it as a sequence rather than just saying 'I fixed it.' First, I don't get defensive -- I thank whoever caught it, since catching a bad number before it drove a bad decision is a good thing. Then I go find the specific number in question and trace it step by step back through the query or model, rather than guessing what might be wrong. Most of the time it ends up being one of a handful of usual suspects -- a join that fanned out and inflated a total, a filter excluding rows it shouldn't have, or a measure aggregating the wrong way. Once I've actually found and fixed the root cause, I verify the corrected number against something I trust, and then I go back to whoever flagged it and explain plainly what was wrong and what's different now. If any real decision was made based on the bad number, I make sure that gets flagged too, since that matters more than the report itself. And afterward, I try to add some kind of sanity check or test so the same category of mistake gets caught automatically next time instead of relying on someone noticing it by eye again.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive or dismissive when the issue is first flagged instead of focusing on resolution
Guessing at the cause instead of systematically tracing the specific number back through the logic
Fixing the number without verifying the fix against a known-correct value
Not checking whether any real decisions were made based on the incorrect numbers
keyPoints: Respond calmly and focus on resolution, not blame
Trace the specific discrepancy back through the logic rather than guessing
Verify the fix against a trusted value before declaring it resolved
Communicate clearly what was wrong, what changed, and flag any affected decisions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a calm, methodical investigation process
Identifies plausible real root causes
Addresses communication and verification of the fix

questions.title: Learning a new BI tool quickly
questions.prompt: You've mostly worked in Power BI, and your new team needs you to start building dashboards in Tableau within a couple of weeks. How would you approach ramping up quickly without producing low-quality work in the meantime?
questions.modelAnswer: A good approach leans on transferable concepts rather than starting from zero: the underlying ideas -- dimensions vs. measures, aggregation, filtering, relationships between tables -- are largely the same across Power BI and Tableau, even though the terminology and interface differ (Tableau's discrete/continuous pill distinction maps roughly onto how Power BI treats categorical vs. numeric fields, for instance). I'd start by rebuilding something I already know well in Power BI as a Tableau exercise, since having a known-correct answer to check against is faster than learning entirely new material from scratch. I'd also be upfront with the team about where I am in the ramp-up rather than quietly pretending full fluency, and I'd ask to pair with or get a review from someone already fluent in Tableau on my first few real dashboards, so mistakes specific to Tableau's quirks get caught before they reach end users rather than after.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to learn Tableau as if it were a totally foreign tool, because a lot of what I already know transfers directly -- the concept of a measure, a dimension, a relationship between tables, filtering logic -- Tableau just has its own vocabulary and UI for those same ideas. My first move would be picking something I've already built well in Power BI and rebuilding it in Tableau, since I'll immediately notice where my instincts are wrong because I have a known-correct result to compare against. I'd also just be honest with my team about where I am in that ramp-up rather than pretending I'm already fluent, and I'd specifically ask someone who already knows Tableau well to review my first couple of real dashboards before they go out, so any Tableau-specific mistake gets caught by someone who'd recognize it immediately instead of surfacing later when a stakeholder notices something looks off.
commonMistakes: Assuming a new BI tool requires learning everything from scratch instead of leaning on transferable concepts
Hiding uncertainty about tool fluency instead of being upfront with the team
Shipping unreviewed work during the ramp-up period instead of getting an early review from someone experienced in the new tool
Not using a 'known answer' exercise (rebuilding something already understood) to accelerate learning
keyPoints: Identify which concepts transfer directly versus what's genuinely new terminology/UI
Use a known-correct rebuild exercise to learn faster and catch wrong assumptions
Be transparent with the team about current fluency level during ramp-up
Get an early review from someone experienced in the new tool before work ships

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies transferable concepts rather than treating it as starting from zero
Describes a concrete learning strategy
Addresses quality control during the ramp-up period

questions.title: Prioritizing competing requests
questions.prompt: Two different stakeholders each ask you for a report by end of day, and you genuinely can't finish both. How would you decide what to do and how would you communicate it?
questions.modelAnswer: The instinct to quietly try to do both and risk doing neither well is the wrong move -- the right first step is surfacing the conflict immediately rather than silently struggling with it until the deadline arrives. I'd reach out to both stakeholders (or my manager, if there's a clear chain for prioritization calls) as soon as I realize the conflict exists, not at 4:45pm, explain the situation plainly, and ask or propose which one is more urgent based on what I know about downstream impact -- is one feeding a board meeting tomorrow morning while the other is for an internal check-in that could slip a day. If I can't get a clear answer quickly, I'd propose a reasonable default myself rather than leaving both stakeholders waiting on each other's decision, and I'd give the one that slips an honest, specific new timeline rather than a vague 'soon.' The common thread is transparency early, rather than surprise late.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I realize I can't actually do both well by end of day, I'd flag it immediately rather than sitting on it and hoping I'll somehow find the time. I'd go to both stakeholders, or my manager if there's an obvious person who should make the call, lay out the conflict plainly, and ask which one is actually more time-sensitive -- sometimes one of them doesn't even realize the other request exists, and once they know, the priority sorts itself out pretty fast. If neither answers quickly enough and I have to make the call myself, I'd weigh which one has a harder downstream deadline, like something feeding directly into a meeting that can't move, and go with that. Whatever I decide, I give the other person a real, specific new time I'll have it to them, not a vague 'I'll get to it soon,' because a clear new commitment is a lot easier for someone to plan around than silence.
commonMistakes: Trying to quietly do both and risking a rushed, lower-quality result on each
Waiting until the deadline is imminent to raise the conflict instead of flagging it early
Making the prioritization call without any input from the stakeholders or a manager when one was available
Giving a vague 'I'll get to it soon' instead of a specific new commitment to the deprioritized request
keyPoints: Surface the conflict early, not at the last minute
Ask the stakeholders or manager for input on relative urgency rather than guessing in isolation
Make a reasonable call yourself if a clear answer isn't available quickly
Give a specific new commitment to the deprioritized request instead of a vague timeline

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes surfacing the conflict early and transparently
Describes a reasonable method for deciding priority
Addresses clear communication of the resulting timeline

questions.title: Explaining a DAX measure to a non-technical stakeholder
questions.prompt: A sales manager keeps asking why a DAX measure on your dashboard shows a different number than what they expected, and they have no SQL or DAX background. How would you explain it to them in a way that actually lands?
questions.modelAnswer: The right approach drops the technical vocabulary entirely and explains it in terms of what the number actually represents in their world, not how the formula works mechanically. Instead of saying 'CALCULATE overwrites the filter context,' I'd say something like, 'this number is specifically filtered to only count deals that closed this quarter, which is why it's smaller than the total pipeline number you might be thinking of' -- translating the technical mechanism into the business meaning behind it. I'd also validate their expectation rather than dismissing it -- asking what number they expected and why often reveals that they're thinking of a genuinely different metric (total pipeline vs. closed-won revenue, for instance), which means the real conversation isn't about DAX at all, it's about making sure both of us agree on what the metric is supposed to represent. If the measure turns out to actually be wrong, I'd say so plainly rather than over-explaining a bug as if it were intentional behavior.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start by explaining DAX at all -- I'd start by asking what number they expected to see and why, because half the time that question reveals we're actually talking about two different metrics, not a bug. If it turns out the measure is working correctly, I'd explain it in plain business terms, something like 'this specific number only counts deals that actually closed this quarter, not everything still in the pipeline,' rather than walking them through CALCULATE and filter context, which won't mean anything to them and isn't actually what they're asking about. If I dig in and the measure actually is wrong, I just say that directly instead of trying to explain away a real bug as if it were intentional -- that's a different conversation, and trying to talk around it instead of owning it tends to erode trust a lot faster than just admitting the mistake would.
commonMistakes: Explaining the technical DAX mechanism instead of translating it into business meaning
Not asking what number the stakeholder expected, missing that they might mean a different metric entirely
Assuming the measure must be correct and getting defensive instead of actually checking
Over-explaining a genuine bug in technical terms instead of plainly acknowledging it
keyPoints: Translate the technical mechanism into plain business meaning
Ask what the stakeholder expected to see and why, before explaining anything
Check whether they're actually referring to a different metric entirely
If the measure genuinely has a bug, acknowledge it plainly rather than over-explaining

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains in plain business terms, not technical jargon
Checks the stakeholder's expectation before assuming the cause
Handles the possibility of a genuine bug honestly

questions.title: Receiving critical feedback on your SQL
questions.prompt: A senior data engineer reviews a query you wrote and points out it's inefficient and poorly structured in front of the rest of the team. How do you respond in the moment, and what do you do afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats the feedback as useful information rather than a personal attack, even if the delivery felt blunt or public -- getting defensive or arguing in the moment tends to escalate an uncomfortable moment rather than resolve it, and it signals to the team that feedback isn't welcome, which discourages others from being direct too. In the moment, the right response is something like genuinely asking a clarifying question about the specific concern -- what exactly is inefficient, is it the join structure, the lack of an index-friendly filter, something else -- which shows I'm actually listening rather than just waiting for the criticism to end. Afterward, I'd follow up privately if the public delivery felt harsh, not to relitigate who was right, but because a private conversation about how feedback lands is a reasonable thing to raise separately from the technical content itself. I'd also actually apply the feedback -- rewriting the query, understanding why the new version is better, and treating it as something to remember for next time rather than a one-off fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, my first reaction is to just listen and ask a clarifying question about whatever specifically they think is inefficient, rather than getting defensive about it in the moment, even if it's a little uncomfortable being critiqued in front of the team. Getting into an argument right there usually doesn't help anyone and tends to make the room tenser than it needs to be. After that, I'd actually go rewrite the query based on what they pointed out and make sure I understand why the new version is better, not just copy a fix without learning from it. If the way it was delivered publicly genuinely bothered me, I'd bring that up with them separately afterward, one-on-one, not as a complaint about being wrong, but just as feedback on how it landed -- those are two different conversations and I wouldn't mix them together in the moment.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive or arguing with the feedback in the moment instead of asking a clarifying question
Treating public critical feedback as a personal attack rather than useful technical information
Fixing the immediate query without actually understanding why the new approach is better
Avoiding ever addressing how the feedback was delivered, if it genuinely felt harsh, instead of raising it separately and privately
keyPoints: Respond to critical feedback with curiosity, not defensiveness
Ask clarifying questions to understand the specific concern
Actually apply and internalize the fix, not just patch the immediate symptom
Address delivery concerns separately and privately from the technical content

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a non-defensive, professional in-the-moment response
Describes genuinely learning from and applying the feedback
Addresses delivery concerns appropriately and separately
